newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Snow forecast for Rio's Ipanema beach.
newsitem.headline: Snow forecast for Rio's Ipanema beach.

text.p: At least 95 tonnes of snow is forecast to fall on Brazil's world famous Ipanema beach in September -- when the world's top snowboarders will mingle with Rio's surf and sun crowd.
Brazilians, many of whom have never seen snow, will be able to lounge on the beach while watching snowboarders fly across an icy ramp with a tropical backdrop.

The Ipanema "snowstorm" is the dream of Rio orthopedist and snowboarding fan Leonardo Metsavaht, 33, who has been scheming and planning for 18 months to stage the world's first international snowboarding competition on a tropical beach.

"They've held snowboard competitions in cities like Milan and Paris, but never on a beach, let alone in a tropical country," Metsavaht told Reuters on Friday. "A snow ramp on the seashore with islands in the background, that's the image that inspired me."
The Ipanema championship scheduled for Sept. 21 is part of the official circuit of the International Snowboard Federation and will involve at least 16 of the world's best snowboarders.

They will compete in the category known as "big air" or "straight jump" in which snowboarders reach speeds of 25-30 mph (40-50 kph) as they take off from a ramp to jump as high as 42 feet (13 metres).

The beach ramp, 49 feet (15 metres) high, 164 feet (50 metres) long and 65 feet (20 metres) wide, will be covered with 20 inches (50 cm) of "real snow" in the middle of the Brazilian spring when temperatures can easily reach 28-30 Celsius (82-86 Fahrenheit).
"We have the technology to produce snow in any type of climate," Metsavaht said. "It would take two to three days for all the snow on the ramp to melt."
The snowboard extravaganza, which is being sponsored by several companies, will cost about $1 million and is expected to attract 20,000 spectators.
There will be bleachers for 3,000 invited guests, but most spectators will camp out in the sand, which is the "true charm" of the event, according to Metsavaht.
He also plans a 330 square foot (100 square metres) snow pit to let people build snowmen and have snowball fights.
The snow is produced by mixing air with water under great pressure, effectively evaporating the water which is then immediately mixed with freezing cold liquid nitrogen.
Metsavaht's snow dreams don't stop there. He also wants to build a permanent indoor ski slope in Rio de Janeiro.
